source: Ferguson & Sanford (2008) Anomalies in real and counterfactual worlds: an eye-movement investigation
finding: Human readers set up a counterfactual world from an 'if' premise. Real-world violations stop being a problem when the context licenses them. Yet real-world violations still cause early difficulty whatever the context.
numbers: Three eye-tracking studies; 2x2 design (context CW vs RW x second sentence RW-anomalous vs RW-congruent). Sample sizes and reading times not seen (repository page gives abstract only).
quote: Real-world violations caused early difficulty regardless of prior context
limits: Abstract-only page was read, not the full paper. Numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: A scoped hypothetical space works, but real-world knowledge is still checked first. The agent should expect a leak from the base world into a scoped space and test for it.

source: Ferguson, Scheepers & Sanford (2010) Expectations in counterfactual and theory of mind reasoning
finding: Two visual-world eye-tracking studies. Both counterfactual and false-belief contexts give an early anticipatory look to the context-supported referent. Integrating facts that clash with the counterfactual is delayed. This delay is absent in false-belief contexts.
numbers: Exp 1 counterfactual context, Exp 2 false-belief context. Sample sizes not seen.
limits: Abstract-only page. Shows counterfactual and belief spaces behave differently in humans, so they are not one mechanism.
agent_relevance: Do not treat hypothesis space and another-person-belief space as the same container type. Counterfactual spaces cost more to keep apart from fact.

source: Li, Yu & Ettinger (2023) Counterfactual reasoning: testing language models' understanding of hypothetical scenarios
finding: Five pretrained LMs (GPT-2, GPT-3, BERT, RoBERTa, MPNet) raise their preference for counterfactual-consistent endings after an 'if' premise, but mostly at or just above chance. Only GPT-3 prefers the counterfactual ending on over 70 percent of items.
numbers: Small set adapted from Ferguson (2012): 96 items. Large synthetic set: 12,960 items. Items right in BOTH the counterfactual and real-world conditions: GPT-3 50.0, RoBERTa 31.3, MPNet 28.1, GPT-2 18.8, BERT 9.4 percent (chance 25).
limits: Pretrained LMs, not instruction-tuned chat models. Prediction by log-probability, not generation.
agent_relevance: A plain model needs an explicit structural cue (if, suppose) to open a scoped space. It does not reliably hold the space open.

source: Li, Yu & Ettinger (2023) Counterfactual reasoning: testing language models' understanding of hypothetical scenarios (Exp2: cue words)
finding: When the counterfactual premise is followed by 'In reality ...', most models barely change their preference, so they follow lexical triggers (e.g. 'vegetarians' pulls 'cabbages') rather than the scope. Only GPT-3 drops much, and only on the large synthetic set.
numbers: Drop from counterfactual to counterfactual-then-reality condition was small for most models; GPT-3 showed a substantial drop on the 12,960-item set only.
quote: Most models are largely following simpler lexical triggers
limits: Exp3 marker test: with tense and connective cues varied, only GPT-3 showed substantial preference for the logical continuation; GPT-3 sensitivity depends on linear distance (Appendix A.4).
agent_relevance: Leakage by word association is the main failure mode of scoped spaces. S2 needs a code check that a claim made inside a space is not reused outside it.

source: Li, Yu & Ettinger (2023) Counterfactual reasoning: testing language models' understanding of hypothetical scenarios (world knowledge helps)
finding: Stronger world knowledge went with better counterfactual override. Models that knew the real fact best were best at overriding it under 'if'.
numbers: Significant Pearson correlation between item-level strength of world knowledge (baseline-bias condition) and counterfactual preference strength, for all five LMs (values in Appendix A.3, not extracted).
limits: Correlational. Cuts against the simple idea that strong priors block scoped override.
agent_relevance: Strong priors are not a reason to skip scoping. A clear 'if' frame can still work on well-known facts.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks
finding: Across 11 tasks, GPT-4 and others do far worse in a counterfactual world (changed rules) than in the default world, even when they pass a check that they understand the changed rule.
numbers: Two-digit addition, GPT-4 no CoT, 1,000 items: base 10 = 100.0, base 9 = 23.4, base 11 = 38.4, base 8 = 82.3, base 16 = 63.0 percent. With 0-shot CoT: base 10 = 98.2, base 9 = 38.6, base 11 = 56.5. Counterfactual comprehension check (200 items): base 9 = 90.0, base 11 = 91.0 percent.
limits: Tasks chosen so the changed world is rare, not alien. Some changes are harder in themselves (base-9 carry), so part of the gap may be difficulty, not memorising.
agent_relevance: A model can state a scoped rule yet not apply it. Spaces that change rules need an executed check (code), not the model's own statement.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks (moderators)
finding: The gap shrinks when the counterfactual world is more common (bases 8 and 16 beat 9 and 11; drop-D guitar tuning beats other tunings) and when it is nearer the default. Few-shot examples help but do not close it.
numbers: Arithmetic few-shot CoT up to 16 examples: gap reduced but still substantial for bases 9, 11, 16; gains plateau near 16-shot. Default and counterfactual accuracy correlate across task variants.
limits: Correlations not shown causal (authors' own footnote). Few-shot test run on arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Expect scoped spaces with unusual rules to fail more than ones with familiar rules. Give worked examples in the space, but do not rely on them alone.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks (qualitative drawing)
finding: In the drawing task GPT-4 passes the check that it understands flip or rotate, but often draws the object unchanged, or draws a worse object.
numbers: Vertical flip, 90 and 180 degree rotation conditions; error analysis on examples (house, penguin unchanged; unicorn, cake degraded).
limits: Qualitative, small set of examples.
agent_relevance: The scope instruction can be understood and still ignored at execution time.

source: Kim & Schuster (2023) Entity tracking in language models
finding: Tracking what each box holds after a chain of moves is a minimal state-of-a-space task. Only text-davinci-003, which was trained on code, beat a strong random baseline. Flan-T5 and GPT-3 davinci mostly repeated the initial state.
numbers: text-davinci-003 still gave the full correct box contents after 7 operations in over 25 percent of cases. Accuracy fell as operations increased. A probe on the initial state alone reaches 62.7 percent in a naive design, which is why trivial cases are removed.
limits: Synthetic box world. Appendix reports GPT-4 does better (Fig 8, exact value not extracted).
agent_relevance: Tracking state per container degrades with the number of updates. S2 should keep the state in code (one record per space), not in the model's memory.

source: Kim & Schuster (2023) Entity tracking in language models (finetuned T5)
finding: Finetuned T5 can learn entity tracking, but it generalises poorly when the test differs from training (more operations, other surface forms, ambiguous reference).
numbers: Base split near perfect; accuracy falls on NumOps, AltForm and AmbiRef splits (one split gives the correct final state in under about 55 percent of cases; exact per-split values not extracted).
limits: Small T5 models; synthetic data.
agent_relevance: Training on tracking is brittle. Hard-coded state beats learned state for an agent.

source: Prakash et al. (2024) Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms: a case study on entity tracking
finding: Models track entities by tracking the position of the right entity in context. Fine-tuned versions (Vicuna, Goat, FLoat on Llama-7B) use the same circuit. Gains come from better handling of the position signal and better retrieval of the value.
numbers: Circuit restores at least 88 percent of the full fine-tuned model performance. Goat-7B value-fetcher heads about 20 percent better than Llama-7B.
limits: Open 7B models, templated box tasks.
agent_relevance: Tracking is positional, so many near-identical containers in one prompt invite collisions. Keep few, labelled spaces.

source: Feng & Steinhardt (2024) How do language models bind entities in context?
finding: Mechanism for binding things to scopes: models attach a binding ID vector to each entity and each attribute. Swapping these vectors switches what the model believes the pairing is. IDs sit in a continuous subspace, so nearby IDs are confused.
numbers: LLaMA-13B, 500 samples, n=2 groups: accuracy above 99 percent with no intervention, below 3 percent after attribute or entity swap, above 97 percent after both swaps cancel. Random vectors of same size have no effect. Found in every sufficiently large Pythia and LLaMA model.
limits: Open models only; section 5 notes limits on generality.
agent_relevance: Gives a cause for scope leakage: binding capacity is limited, so many parallel spaces blur. Cap the number of live spaces.

source: Zhu, Zhang & Wang (2024) Language models represent beliefs of self and others
finding: Whose-belief-is-it is linearly readable inside Mistral-7B. The model's own (oracle) belief is easy to decode. The protagonist's belief is found only in a small set of middle-layer attention heads (over 80 percent probe accuracy). Pushing activations along the learned direction raises false-belief accuracy.
numbers: Probes per attention head; binary chance 50 percent, quaternary chance 25 percent; selected heads tested against a 75 percent baseline. Steering raises false-belief accuracy and slightly lowers true-belief accuracy (partly more invalid answers).
limits: Mistral-7B and similar open models, templated stories. Probe success does not prove the model uses it as a scoped space.
agent_relevance: There is an internal slot for someone else's view. It is thin, so an agent should write each space out in text and code, not rely on it.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) Minding language models' (lack of) theory of mind: SymbolicToM
finding: Closest AI test of the S2 idea. Keeping an explicit graph of each character's belief, and each character's belief about others' beliefs, and giving the model only the relevant slice, lifts off-the-shelf models by large margins with no training.
numbers: ToMi: +62 points first-order false belief for Flan-T5-XL; +78 points second-order false belief for GPT-3.5; on a GPT-4 comparison subset Flan-T5-XL gains +76 and +36 points; reality and memory questions stay near perfect (small declines for Flan-T5-XL).
limits: ToMi is template based; SymbolicToM relies on NLI and a parser that may fail on hard text. Works for belief tracking, not general hypothesis spaces.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2: a program holds the scoped spaces, the model sees only one slice at a time. Generalisation beyond ToMi is untested.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) Minding language models' (lack of) theory of mind: SymbolicToM (robustness)
finding: On a paraphrased test the supervised models collapse while the symbolic scaffold with a base model holds up.
numbers: ParaphrasedToMi: TTT average accuracy down 54 points; finetuned GPT-3 down about 40 on false-belief questions; SymbolicToM-equipped models keep high accuracy.
limits: Gains depend on the quality of the symbolic parse.
agent_relevance: A scaffold transfers where training does not.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the logic of the false-belief task (transparent container, agent can see inside, relabelled container) flip GPT-3.5 answers to the wrong ones. This is a failed extension of the claim of robust ToM.
numbers: Original prompts: P(chocolate) 95 to 99 percent as expected. Altered variants show wrong answers, e.g. popcorn 58 percent vs chocolate 36 percent in one alteration; cat-in-box variants go from 0 to 3 percent wrong-location in the original to 25 to 43 percent in altered ones.
limits: Only GPT-3.5 and a handful of hand-made variants; no N.
agent_relevance: A scoped belief space must track access conditions, not just who thinks what.

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or neural theory of mind? Stress testing social reasoning in large language models
finding: Six ToM tasks and an adversarial set. Models do well on standard false-belief stories and badly on adversarial ones. Newer models can do worse on some adversarial types.
numbers: Unexpected-transfer false-belief subset: GPT-4 97 percent. Other person: 93.8 percent (davinci-002) to 68.8 (GPT-4). 'inon' type: 71.4 to 0 percent. Transparent access: 66.7 to 0 percent. Unexpected contents: GPT-4 97.5 and 83.3 percent on two categories. FauxPas-EAI: GPT-4 27 percent.
limits: Multiple-choice and generative probing give slightly different numbers.
agent_relevance: Adversarial cases are exactly where scoped belief fails; build them into the agent's test set.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS)
finding: Positive side of the debate: 11 LLMs on false-belief tasks. Older models solved none. GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5 about 20 percent. ChatGPT-4 75 percent, close to 6-year-old children.
numbers: 40 tasks, each with a false-belief scenario, 3 control scenarios and reversed versions; the model must solve all prompts of a task; ChatGPT-4 solved 75 percent of tasks.
limits: Ullman and Shapira later broke similar results with trivial alterations; text may hold shallow cues.
agent_relevance: Headline success on templated tasks overstates scoped-belief skill.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context
finding: One irrelevant sentence drops accuracy sharply: a leak of out-of-scope content into the reasoning. Fixes that work: self-consistency, exemplars that include distractors, and an instruction to ignore irrelevant context.
numbers: GSM-IC: of problems solved by baseline, no more than 18 percent solved for every distractor type; fewer than 30 percent of base problems solved consistently after distractors. Self-consistency with 20 samples: +11 points micro accuracy overall, +35.5 on 0-CoT; 99.7 percent recall of the right answer in 20 samples; best macro accuracy only 45 percent. Role-overlap distractors hurt most (macro accuracy 0 for text-davinci-003 on problems over 2 steps).
limits: Arithmetic only, 2023 models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003).
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that scoping context matters. Putting only the relevant slice in each call is cheap.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive chameleon or stubborn sloth: LLMs in knowledge conflicts
finding: When context contradicts what the model knows, models accept the context if it is coherent and convincing. But if the context also holds something that matches their memory, they show strong confirmation bias and keep their old belief.
numbers: GPT-4 memorisation ratio about 80 percent on the most popular entities. Order of evidence swings results by over 5 points, and by over 30 points for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B.
limits: Evidence order effects differ per model.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis in a space must be isolated from base-world memory; mixing in even partly matching text brings back the prior.

source: Fauconnier (1985/1994) Mental Spaces: aspects of meaning construction in natural language
finding: Founding claim: language builds small temporary spaces (belief, time, hypothetical, picture) with links between them. Not checked this session; no numbers.
limits: Theory with no experiment of its own. Evidence comes from the psycholinguistic and LLM work above.
agent_relevance: S2 is a design analogy, not an empirically validated mechanism.

source: Nieuwland & Martin (2012) If the real world were irrelevant, so to speak (ERP study of counterfactual comprehension)
finding: Recalled, not opened: brain responses show readers use counterfactual context quickly, in line with Ferguson & Sanford. Numbers not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: scope and world knowledge compete.

source: Search note: no study found that tests Fauconnier-style mental spaces as a prompting method
finding: No direct test of mental spaces as an LLM method was found. arXiv abstract searches returned nothing and OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited. Nearest tests are counterfactual, belief-tracking and entity-tracking studies above.
numbers: 0 direct hits in the searches that returned results.
limits: Search was limited, not exhaustive.
agent_relevance: Label S2 as [D] design choice with indirect support.
